utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a reason why our LiveNote on the laptops is not on? Anyway, let's move. In the meantime, you will look into it or someone comes up to look into it so that we don't waste time. We can follow the transcript on the main monitor. Is that okay with you? All right. Is your laptop working properly?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat. Appearances. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Julian Nicholls, with Joanna Korner, and Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Cunningham with Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Welcome back. Today you are going to be cross-examined by Mr. Nicholls for the Prosecutor. My word of advice to you is to keep your answers as concise and as precise as they were when you were being examined by Mr. Cunningham. It will make sure that you will be out of this courtroom by the end of today's business. One other thing that I need to advise you upon is that in accordance and pursuant to the oath that you took yesterday, to speak the truth, the whole truth -- it's not just me. You have an obligation to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, not only when you're being asked by the lawyer -- by the Defence team that brought you here, but also when you are being cross-examined by the opposite party, by the other party. That's the Prosecution. So your obligation stays. And in fact, the usher is now going to approach you once more with the text of your solemn declaration which you are kindly asked to repeat. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may sit down. That was of yesterday probably. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, sorry about these minor interruptions, but sometimes we mark what we have on the laptop, and as we were, we couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Take your time. There's no hurry. You have got the whole morning sitting for yourself if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I read the transcript yesterday and I think it may be even shorter than I thought beforehand. I'm sorry, could the ELMO please be moved somehow. I can't see the witness's face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that fine with you, Ms. Korner, as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're going to try to finish today as quickly as possible. As you did with Mr. Cunningham, many questions will be answerable with a yes or no and that's usually the best way to answer. The Judge also reminded you about the oath, and I think you told the truth yesterday as best you could. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you have been interviewed by the Defence before in this case, I imagine, probably in Banja Luka and also here in The Hague, and you told them the truth when you --

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you told them the truth when you answered their questions, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in addition you spoke with an attorney from our office, an investigator. You alluded to that yesterday. In July of 2001, and when you spoke with them, you told them the truth as best you could, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told the truth, and that was in July, but also in September 1992 in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, that was in 2001 that I'm speaking of, July 2001, you were spoken with by members of our office.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had two interviews with your representatives. One interview was shorter than the other. And I believe that it was -- yes, you're right, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just take you, because I think you put it nicely, the last page of your interview, that should come up on Sanction. And if you like, I can give you a copy in your language with the portions highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're having copies made. I thought they had been made. There was a miscommunication just in case the Sanction doesn't work perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is. You have to press, Mr. Cunningham, you have to press "computer evidence" to see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'll just read the portion I'm interested in and you can tell me if that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which page are you referring to, Mr. Nicholls? Which one of the two, the first or the second?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The one on the left is B/C/S, the right is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And because it's difficult to read, I'll read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were asked at about line 15 if you had anything to add at the end of the interview. And your response was this: "No, I don't think that any of the questions were unclear in any way. I think that everything was clarified, and I did try to give you the most candid answers I could and tell you exactly what happened. My own profession dictates that I tell you what I know, so I have no questions, I have no remarks. What I knew, I told you." Now, that's true, isn't it? That was a true statement by you?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we may have some more -- well, we will probably have some more times that we refer to this document. At the moment, I'm going to look at page 3. Sir, if you could look at -- that's page 3 in the English. Sir, if you could open your version to the page, on the top it will have the number L0110415. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you having problems, Mr. Cunningham, with following the document? And your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No. Judge, we're having no problems, it's just small print.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, I know. At our age, at my age in particular, it starts to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As I said, copies are on the way, hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, on page of this interview, you were asked as a sort of preliminary question whether you had been asked to be a witness by the Defence. And this was your answer in July 2001: "Yes, they asked me if I would be a witness for Mr. Brdjanin. But since I never worked in the team with Mr. Brdjanin, and I never attended a single meeting of the Crisis Staff, I declined the offer of becoming a witness for him because I had nothing to say in his defence. I have nothing to say whatsoever. I don't have the actual information. I told them this, well, about a year and a half ago, even more, and no one's asked me again." Now, the question is -- is that what it says in your version, in your language?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, there, I think what you were saying was, one, that you didn't work closely with Brdjanin in 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it may be said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And also you were saying there that you really had no idea what went on in ARK Crisis Staff meetings. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move on to another topic now. You don't need to keep looking at that document. You told us you graduated from law school in 1964. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Since that time, have you obtained any advanced legal degrees, any further diplomas, Ph.D.'s, any kind of further qualifications in law?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just passed some exams.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was right after you graduated. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For administrative law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I did my bar exam later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've told us as well that your work as a secretary in the municipality was essentially an administrative task. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: More administrative, and it also had a lot to do with legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just read something you said in your interview. This is on page 7. I don't know if we necessarily need to put it up. Let's see if you agree this is correct. "My duties as a secretary were more administrative. My task was to -- after the decisions or conclusions were prepared by the government or by the Executive Committee were made. I was supposed to copy that, prepare it all, call a session of the assembly with Mr. Radic, and make sure that each of the delegates had their material, secure the premises where the session would be held and to attend the session. To work with Mr. Radic on preserving the normality of the session, that was basically what I did." Is that a fair statement of your duties?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I believe one of your duties was editing the minutes and preparing the minutes.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said I think several times yesterday that you were never a member of any ARK Crisis Staff. In fact, you were never asked to be the secretary of either the municipal Crisis Staff in Banja Luka or the regional Crisis Staff, were you?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And by "yes," you mean that you were not ever invited to be a secretary for those bodies?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm answering your question. It's true that nobody ever asked me, nor did I ever go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm curious about this: Did you ever edit the Prijedor municipal Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to just show the witness P1407. That is the Official Gazette of the Municipality of Prijedor, year 1, number 3, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, this isn't a trick question or anything, I just want you to look at the last page of that, the very bottom of the last page. On my copy in English, it states: "The Official Gazette is published by the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. It is edited by the technical services editor, Branko Cvijic."

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, where are you reading this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It should be at the very bottom of the last page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says in my copy is Dusan Baltic, editor-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- the copy that we have, Mr. Nicholls, at least Judge Janu who reads the language, at least the Cyrillic script, is confirming to me that what the witness said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do these mistakes happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know this-- what happened, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've seen it happen over and over again, unfortunately, as with the names of the original ARK Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't blame you. I mean, I would react exactly myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I often check them myself. With the Cyrillic, but it's clear here, and I just wanted to ask the witness if he was the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would see no reason why I would have to go and double check with the original. Because this is not a misspelled name. It's a completely different person. All right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry about that. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, sir. I just wanted to clear that up. And it has been. I want to now turn to a different topic, something you spoke of -- a lot of time yesterday on, which are the Crisis Staffs which appeared in 1992. Now, the Banja Luka Municipal Crisis Staff, you were asked about that in 2001. And a couple years ago in 2001, you weren't aware of who all the members of the Banja Luka Municipal Crisis Staff were. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you remember being shown a Glas article, which is actually P137 for reference, and your comment on that was: "I didn't know that the police, the army, and the police were represented to such a degree on the staff." Do you remember that, or do you want to look at the documents?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need to look at the documents. I really didn't know that the army and the police were so represented. But it was put to me, and I later checked it and found out that indeed on every staff, there was a representative of the army and a representative of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: One representative, but I hadn't known that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk a little bit -- we might come back to the municipal Crisis Staff, but now I'm asking you some questions -- we're going to change. I'm talking about the ARK regional Crisis Staff. Now, in 1992, General Momir Talic was a fairly important person in the Banja Luka area. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So was Predrag Radic because of his positions as you outlined yesterday?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So was Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Stojan Zupljanin was chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Vojo Kupresanin was also a pretty important man in the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't say that, really. He made himself out to be more important than he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, he held an important position.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. He was president of the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you also know, don't you, that all of these men were on the ARK Crisis Staff? They were members, along with Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So when you said yesterday that anybody could proclaim themselves anything they wanted to be in relation to the ARK Crisis Staff, to be fair, it really wasn't just anybody who proclaimed themselves or who became the ARK Crisis Staff; it was the local political, military, and police leadership, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were, thanks to their positions and the duties they discharged, so they were appointed ex officio, including the president of the court, the district prosecutor, and the dean of the university, although his position seems unrelated. But nevertheless...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, you've answered that question. Thank you. Now, you also said yesterday when talking about the ARK and reading some statutes which Defence counsel showed you that you didn't consider it statutorily authorised or legal. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed that these people could not pass decisions or laws with legal effect until the moment they are ratified by Municipal Assembly. I am here talking about some relationships. I didn't say anything about any specific issues because I don't know anything about any specific issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll try to avoid too many specific issues, then, if you don't feel competent to talk about them. One of the -- let me put it to you this way: Regardless of whether -- of your answer now, the Crisis Staffs, including the ARK Crisis Staff, enjoyed the support of the top SDS leadership, men like Karadzic and Krajisnik, didn't it -- didn't they?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So even if they didn't have a sort of legal authority, they had a -- kind of inherent authority since they were supported by the top SDS leadership at that time, regardless of the technical legality.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking as a lawyer, a person from the profession. I know what their competencies were. Now, whether they had something that went beyond their competencies, I can't talk about that. But it is true that they enjoyed the support of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I want to talk just a little bit now about the minutes that were kept by different bodies during this time. You've already stated that one of your duties was to keep the minutes and to preserve them. Correct, of your Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipal Assembly sessions were recorded, audiorecorded. There was a person who did that. And after the sessions, I would do transcripts, and I would do excerpts from the minutes. The audiotapes were preserved, and I compiled excerpts from those tapes, together with the person in charge of those tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And from reading your interview, I got the impression - you tell me if I was right or wrong - that you viewed that task very seriously and you were scrupulous in trying to keep the important information that ended up contained in those minutes.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But we are talking only about the sessions of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. Only the sessions where that was your specific duty. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know where those minutes and tapes are now?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that was left when I left in the Municipal Assembly building in Room Number 67. Nowadays, this whole thing has been dismantled, and this particular room houses another person's office. All those documents were then archived, but I don't know where. But I am -- I believe that everything has been archived; however, not in that same room where it was when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you believe that they're in the same building, though?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the secretary -- well, tell me if you remember. What was Boro Blagojevic's function in 1992 as a secretary?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boro Blagojevic was the secretary of the ARK Krajina Assembly. He was the only professional working in the ARK Krajina. I believe that he attended all the sessions of the assembly, of the Executive Board, and of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, one of the points in your interview, talking about how you kept minutes, you stated that Mr. Blagojevic -- you didn't know how he kept the minutes, whether he tape recorded them or transcribed them, but that he had to have kept them. That's how things were done. Do you still agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you have any idea where those minutes are archived today?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to now talk about another short subject. You've brought it up yourself already, verification. Did you know -- do you know that the ARK Assembly verified the decisions and conclusions of the Crisis Staff on 17th of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know when sessions took place, what was verified. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I show the witness P285, please. For the record, these are the extracts from the minutes of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina of 17 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, the item I'm interested in having you read is item 4. Could you just read that in your language, please, and tell me when you're done. Now, this is a vote of 98-1, to verify all theses decisions and conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff. That's a pretty strong endorsement by the assembly, wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm done with that document. I'm going to move on to another area. And this is something you also talked about a little bit yesterday, implementation of ARK Crisis Staff conclusions. And first, I'd like you to be given, please, P223 and P227. P227 is the ARK Gazette. I'm interested in the 21st of May decision. That's actually decision number 14 if it makes it easier to find it.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Can you please point me to a certain page? I'm having difficulties finding that particular thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There's no need to apologise. I think the usher can help you. It's decision 14, 21st of May. I'm sorry, I don't have the B/C/S ERN. I can probably find it if it's given to me. The dates are in English -- not in English, but in Latin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you found -- usher, have you found both versions, English and B/C/S? All right, okay. If you have a problem, I can give you mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, I think I've got the B/C/S here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you look at the extract of the minutes of the 77th session of the Executive Committee of Banja Luka Municipality, if you could just read that document, conclusions 1 and 2 to yourself and tell me when you're done. And that's P223.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask the usher to move the English version up a little bit on the ELMO, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read item 1 and item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, looking at the 21st of May 1992 ARK Crisis Staff conclusions, could you read items 1, 2, and 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For the record, now reading from P227.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What both of these documents contain in their conclusions are, one, that all workers absent from work for three days without proper justification will be given notice by the relevant authorities. And two, that sick leave if granted must be strictly examined to make sure that it wasn't an effort to avoid mobilisation or work obligations.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you'd agree with me, wouldn't you, that the conclusions of the 21st of May ARK Crisis Staff meeting are virtually identical to the conclusions of the 1st of June 1992 meeting of the Executive Committee of the Banja Luka Municipality?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we are looking at items 1 and 2 on the first document, and items 1, 2, and 3 on the second document, then yes, they are identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Exactly. And those conclusions on the Executive Committee document would be mandatory, would they not?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should be mandatory. However, I don't know to what extent they were implemented. I don't think that they were ever observed in the very strict way that they were drafted here. But it is correct that according to the labour law which was then in effect and is still in effect, a person who is absent from work for three days without any justification, they can be given a notice. And that stems from the labour law, and this provision of the labour law has been incorporated into both sets of conclusions, and they only somehow stepped up the measures by saying that all the sick leaves will be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there's an example of where you were going way beyond the answer you needed to give to the question. I appreciate you wanting to explain, but the question was whether these were mandatory. And you answered yes, legally in principle, the way you have been speaking about technical legalities, they were. So that's all you really need to say to answer the question. However, you do know that in concrete terms in reality as a result of both of these sets of conclusions, people were dismissed from their employment in 1992. Right?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to P1407 with some trepidation. That is the Prijedor Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'd also like the witness to be given P258 which is an ARK Crisis Staff decision of 19th of June 1992. Sorry, Your Honours, I don't know which list you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is our executives obviously prepared the documents for us based on the document list that was last available, and that was yesterday's. So we don't have 258. I do have 1407. And I say it with trepidation, too, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I apologise that you didn't have them all together in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. It can be solved by putting it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if we look first at P1407 -- well, sorry, let's do it the other way around. First let's look at P258. And what I'd like you to look at it, sir, you can go straight to decision number 45. Just make sure we're looking at the right document, this is the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, first year, number 3.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just to yourself, could you read decision number 45, which states that the proper municipal organs of administration shall be informed of all abandoned property which shall then be proclaimed property of the state and placed at the disposal of Municipal Assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That should be ERN 00389001 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All I need you to do right now, sir, is read that to yourself and let me know when you've read it and understood. Actually, just the first part of that decision 1, of that decision.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to look at Exhibit P1407, the Prijedor Official Gazette. And I'm interested in decision 122, which is: "Decision on the temporary allocation of immoveable property that has been declared state property." Now, you don't need to read that whole decision, sir. I'm most interested in the preamble. It should be on about the second page. It's right at the beginning. It states: "Pursuant to Article 1 of the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina (Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, number 3/92), Article 1 of the decision to declare property that has been abandoned state property..." And it goes on to cite Article 230 of the statute of the Municipality of Prijedor, that this decision is being taken. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And have you read both of those sections?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, again, as a lawyer, wouldn't this be an example to you of an ARK decision being implemented --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've an objection. He's already testified yesterday that he'd never had no knowledge of what was going on in other municipalities. To ask him to comment on this would be rank speculation. I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not speculation. It's not speculation. He's being faced with a document, and he's being asked for his personal opinion on it. He has been giving us personal opinions based on his legal expertise and also administrative expertise. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd also like to say I think that's a mischaracterisation of the evidence yesterday. Mr. Cunningham asked him about Mr. Brdjanin's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time, Mr. Nicholls. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry for that interruption, sir. As a lawyer, you'd agree with me, wouldn't you, that this is an example of an ARK Crisis Staff decision being used and being implemented in the Prijedor Municipality by the Prijedor Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This stems from the preamble of this decision wherein they are citing the decision of the Crisis Staff as the legal foundation as well as the Official Gazette of the Prijedor Municipality. It stems from this that this decision was adopted in keeping with the decision adopted by the ARK Krajina and the statute of Prijedor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the answer to my question, in short - you've explained it well - is yes. This is an example of authority and the implementation of the ARK in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We might be able to make some of this quicker and look at a few less documents. Let me ask you a question. Are you aware that through the ARK Crisis Staff decisions and conclusions in 1992, media personnel, people who worked for Banja Luka Radio and Banja Luka TV, were dismissed from their positions? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really wouldn't be able to tell you that. I know that there were dismissals, but I believe that the dismissals were carried out by the party because at that time, the SDS was very strong in that area. Their personnel policy was being implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me - we'll do this very quickly - go back to P227, the 8th of May decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask Mr. Nicholls which decision number that is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cunningham, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It should be 00497840.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And to tell if we're on the right page, if you look at number 4, sir, it should state: "In the future, the Krajina mass media are to operate according" -- I'm sorry. Number 9 is the one I'm interested in. That may be on the next page. The second paragraph of conclusion number 9 which states: "All management posts in enterprises must be held by persons absolutely loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Have you read that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I haven't. I didn't have -- I haven't found it. If you could help me, please. Yes, yes, that is item 9, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Why don't you read items 9 and 4 to yourself and tell me when you're done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, will Mr. Ackerman be coming here this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If the Court desires his presence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like his presence here to discuss the list of witnesses because I went through it more accurately, and I think he needs to give us some explanations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would require him here, say, at about half 11, 12.00, something like that. What time do you think you will finish, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Probably soon after the break. Soon after the break I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Soon after the break. So he should be here at about 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll call him at the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My guess is about 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You've read those. You were asked about those conclusions during your interview in 2001. And I can show it to you if you want to read your exact answer. You were asked whether or not those were carried out. And your answer was: "I could not tell you right now whether they were implemented to a hundred per cent degree or not." And maybe we could put this on the ELMO. Page 41 in English. "But I've already told you that as far as item 4 is concerned, that the key positions that people were appointed to, the key positions in the media, by the Crisis Staff, and possibly by the SDS -- oh, no, I'm sorry, by the SDS and possibly by the Crisis Staff, and regarding item 9, again, as it's written, I can't tell you that it was fully implemented. But there is no doubt that there were companies that did implement this."

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And today, I could repeat it word for word. What I said is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to now talk a little bit about another topic you spoke about yesterday, which was the Crisis Staff's competence legally or in fact to control or order the police to take certain actions. Okay? And I'd like to give -- have you now look at P227 again.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which particular decision from this Official Gazette do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Conclusion number 7, which is the 11th of May 1992 ARK Crisis Staff conclusion. And the only one I'm really interested in you reading right now is number 1, which concerns the extension of a deadline for the surrender of illegally acquired weapons on the 14th of May 1992 at 2400 hours. Just read all of conclusion number 2 if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If the usher might want to get P202 ready.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the last paragraph of that conclusion number 1 states: "After the deadline expires, weapons will be confiscated by employees of the Security Services Centre of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and severe sanctions will be imposed on those who ignore the call of the Crisis Staff." Correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at P202. This is a Banja Luka security services dispatch dated the 20th of May 1992. And I don't know if it's signed by or has a signature block - I don't have the B/C/S original - but it's attributed to Stojan Zupljanin. What I'd like you to look at specifically, sir, is --

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you to look at item number 23. And while you're reading that, just to clarify so you don't get confused, this is a dispatch dated the 20th of May 1992, but it relates to the conclusions of a meeting held on the 6th of May 1992. So please tell me when you've read section 23. It begins: "In all our activities, we are obliged to observe all measures and apply all procedures ordered by the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region." And then it states: "With regard to disarmament, when the deadline for weapons surrender expires on 11 May 1992, we should take no objection until the Crisis Staff makes the relevant decisions. It is very important that we solve this problem comprehensively, insisting on the disarmament of extremist groups." Tell me when you've finished reading that.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, is that not what we've just put together, an order by the Crisis Staff to the CSB and a recognition by the CSB that it is bound to carry out that order? That's what it is legally, reading these papers as a lawyer. Right?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I did not know about this. However, it does follow from these documents that what you say is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand, sir, and I wasn't trying to imply anything. I fully believe that you've never seen this document before, and I should have prefaced that to you. I know you haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just trying to see if I can shorten my presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were -- completely different topic now. You read yesterday or you were given to read yesterday the statute of the Zobk, as we call it, P2354. I'd ask you to look at that again, and again look at Article 35, would you please, which you read yesterday. And I'll also ask that you be given Exhibit P285. I'm sorry, P258, not 285. P258.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 35 of the statute I have read, and I don't know which decision from this other document you mean. So would you please help me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is decision number 42. This is the decision on the -- on amending and supplementing the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And what that decision of 15 June 1992 states is that paragraph 2 of Article 35 of the statute is amended to read: "The decisions and conclusions of the Assembly must be respected by the municipalities, thereby striking the language, decisions and conclusions of the Assembly shall become binding for the member municipalities once they have been approved by the assemblies of the municipalities." Now, having read that, sir, my only real question is were you aware of that amendment before you just read it now?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I'm seeing this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can comment upon it if you wish me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, that's all right. I just wondered if you'd seen it. But again, from --

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- From a document we looked at earlier, though, if you remember, we know this is one of those decisions and conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff that was, in fact, ratified, as they all were. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if it refers to that assembly meeting which it invokes seemingly 98 to 1 ratio. But I cannot confirm before I compare the two. I cannot know if this is the deadline meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, that's okay. I'm now going to switch topics again completely, talk briefly about something that you also talked about in 2001, and that is the Serbian Defence Forces or SOS in Banja Luka in 1992. Now, in April 1992, you heard of, learned of the SOS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They, in fact, kept you from getting into your own office on the day that the town was blockaded, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it's fair to say that maybe not all, but many of the members of the SOS were criminals?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of them. As it later turned out, most of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And you agree with me that essentially this was a paramilitary force?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it's also true that until our interview in July 2001 when you were shown a document, you didn't know that they were commanded by Nenad Stevandic, did you?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For the record, the document is P400, the report on paramilitaries in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in fact, it wasn't until that interview when you read the Glas article that you knew that Stevandic was a member of the ARK Crisis Staff. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know it until then, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But you did know, and you remembered then, that eventually the SOS became part of the CSB special detachment under the command of Stojan Zupljanin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But I also said that Zupljanin and Talic both dissociated themselves from them, although Talic ended up accepting or admitting a part of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And regardless, you do know that some of these men, the SOS, became part of the special unit which was actually formally under the command of Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could break early, I may have a very short - it's gone more quickly than I expected - I may have something very short after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. My apologies to you, interpreters, please. Let's have a 30-minute break straight away which will make it possible for everyone to reorganise what needs to be reorganised. I require Mr. Ackerman here, the sooner the better. And basically what we are talking about, so that you advise him, is the list of witnesses that we have and the tentative complete list of witnesses that he submitted before and his declaration that he hopes that more or less he should be able to finish the Defence case by the end of January roughly because I find myself in a position where I can hardly understand how that can be possible. So we need to talk about it and see what the true position is. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. The witness I think can leave the courtroom, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he can Your Honour. But just so Mr. Ackerman knows, and Your Honours may want to see where we are on that, for a reason I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reason why I want Mr. Ackerman here is that I have studied these two lists a little bit more carefully, and in the process of doing so I discovered that, for example, Witness Number 9 -- Number 32 who was proposed to come here sometime in November is scheduled to testify for three days here, according to this latest list, but originally he was indicated -- needed only for one day, and that would have included also your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which one was that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness Number 32, and the same for Number 17, four lines up. He is indicated as needing two days now. Before he was indicated as needing half a day, and I want to know where we stand. If he comes here and he finishes the testimony in half a day and we lose the rest of the week, I will get angry, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what I raised the day before yesterday. And Your Honour will recall it all ended unhappily. But can I just mention one specific aspect of the proposed witness list, and that's this: The municipalities not called by the Prosecution and in two cases not investigated. Your Honour, I would like to know sooner rather than later, as I'm sure Your Honours would, whether it is still intended to call witnesses relating to Glamoc, Laktas, Srbac. Because if it is, Your Honour, we will have to do some investigating which will cost this Tribunal more money. And so clearly, if it's not intended now to do this, then I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you can pass on the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And my concern more particularly is that if everything goes according to schedule based on this last list, by the end of the week starting on the 12th of January, Mr. Cunningham, we would have covered 18 witnesses of the Defence which basically subtracted from the 65 that you have indicated would leave us with a number of witnesses that according to your own estimate require 40 days of testimony. And that would take us into March, if not April. And I'm not prepared to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Ackerman said that this list will be reduced and that it doesn't expect all the persons that are mentioned in this list to come over and give testimony. But I think we need to be more articulate and see what the true position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll call him right now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Thanks. 30-minute break

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman, for turning up as requested. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Sorry, I thought about it over the break. I apologise to the witness for bringing you back. I just want to say thank you very much, sir, for being with us here for these last couple days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have any questions either, which basically means that your testimony comes to an end here. On behalf of the Tribunal and on behalf of the Trial Chamber, and that's Judge Janu, Judge Taya, and myself, I should like to thank you for coming over to give evidence, testimony, in this case. The usher will escort you out of the courtroom. And the officers of the Tribunal are available at your disposal should you require any kind of assistance to enable you to return home. On our part, apart from thanking you, we also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you all for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, let me try and explain, Mr. Ackerman, in particular what is worrying me. These -- particularly yesterday, between yesterday and today, I tried to go a little bit deeper into the lists of witnesses you propose to bring over between now and the end of the week in January, starting on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I handed in a new list just a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we're still talking of the week in January starting on the 12th as being the last week that shows up on this document, which basically covers 18 witnesses. If I look at the other list that you had given us before, there are 65 witnesses. So we are left with 43 witnesses that according to your own estimate, based on this document now, the one with the short summary of what the subject of the testimony. If I count it right, which I usually do, gives us -- would give us 40 days of further testimony, which I find it hard to fit in with your previous declaration that you think we should be in a position to finish the case for the Defence towards the end of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that that might be of some concern. Unlike the Prosecution, you've given us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do not expect you -- Mr. Ackerman, I do not expect you to go beyond what you think is the information that you can reveal now because I do understand that you may have one or two or three witnesses that you would like to bring over who are not ready to come over. Similarly, you might come across other witnesses that you would like to bring over which are not even listed here. But I think it's only fair that we are put in a position where we know exactly where we stand because there is no way, if you intend to stick to this list, that we can finish the case for the Defence any time before April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, unlike the Prosecution, you gave us a discrete amount of time to put on the Defence case they were not similarly restricted. But I took you at your word. I believe you were serious about that. So I assure you that the only way we would go beyond that would be for good cause, like the Prosecution did at the end of their case. Clearly, we're not going to be call all 65 of those witnesses. It's not going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But on the other hand, I did not want to list someone who might be a witness just because I didn't want to come under criticism for sneaking witnesses in at the last minute I hadn't told anybody about. So I assure you that we will do the best we can to keep the witness flow going and that we will comply with your end date, unless there is good reason not to by making application to you which you can then decide. But in terms of this list, you must understand, even the list I gave you today, is a very, very soft list in terms of these times because we're still learning as we go how much time these various things are going to take. One of the things that occurs to me, and I'd be interested in your thoughts about it, Your Honour, it occurs to me that by giving us a time limit, you tend to put the Prosecution in a position to control the number of witnesses we can bring because they can simply extend cross-examination and take away time we could bring witnesses. So this might be an appropriate case, because you have given us a deadline, to make an order that the Prosecution cross-examine cannot exceed the direct exam because otherwise they can simply control the amount of time we have to put on witnesses by extending their cross-examinations. That has been done in a number of cases, and I think it might be appropriate in this situation. But the list I've given you today is the best guess we have, and that might change as early as this afternoon. We may decide to bring Witness Number 5 on Monday, 3 November, because it looks like Witness Number 2 may not be able to arrive until that date, and therefore not take the stand until the Tuesday of that week. So we might make that change. In fact, it's fairly likely we will. It depends on whether -- we've got some phone calls in the works right now to try to change some things. But we don't know right now. Otherwise, you know, the list is as good as I can make it right now. It may be that the chances are really good we're going to be moving people up on that list because I think we'll go a little faster than this list contemplates. That's about all I can tell you right now. It's clear that we're not going to call all 65 of those witnesses, but at this point I haven't decided exactly which ones. Now, I understand that Ms. Korner was concerned about the municipalities that were not part of the indictment, that were removed from the indictment -- the only reason, Your Honour, I'll say this again, hopefully for the last time that we would call anybody from any of those municipalities is if we think it's relevant in terms of explaining the relationship between the ARK Crisis Staff and that municipality. We would not under any circumstances call a witness from any of those municipalities to deal with any crime-based issues at all. But I think a witness like that could be relevant just from the standpoint of whether or not the ARK Crisis Staff was significant in any decisions they made in their municipality. So that's a possibility. But I think it's unlikely we'll call anybody from any of those excluded municipalities and we'll certainly -- you can see that we've already given the Prosecution notice well into January, so if we're going to call somebody from any of those municipalities, it would be at least January before that would happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's one thing. Let's clear up all, and then, of course, I will give you the floor, both of you again. And then there is this discrepancy which I'm sure you have an explanation for between the duration, anticipated or expected duration of the testimony of these witnesses, the ones which appear on your list until the week in January starting on the 12th, and it's a discrepancy which also is of some concern to me. For example, if we take Witness Number 17 who is scheduled to come over in the week of 10th of November. Initially he was, according to this document, expected to -- his testimony was expected to last half a day. Then in the list you gave us two days ago, he's shown as testifying for two days. And in the list you handed a few minutes ago, the updated list, he's now moved from 2 to 3 days. The same applies to Witness Number 32, for example, on the week -- in the week of 25th November. He's expected to testify for three days. Now he was anticipated to testify for one day. And we can go on. I mean, Witness Number 50 in the first week of December. I mean, he was initially indicated to come here and testify for half a day. Now it's two days, and knowing who he is, based on previous testimonies and evidence, I think we can easily expect him to be here for three or four days if not an entire week. And we go on and on. So I think, Mr. Ackerman, we need to address this problem a little bit with more - how should I say it - I know we can never be as precise as we would like to be. And also because, for example, today's witness is a classic example. We were anticipating him to last one to two days. And basically if you add the two sessions together, and that could happen with other witnesses as well. But the problem that I have as the Presiding Judge and with the responsibility of coordinating the entire proceedings, the problem is not to have weeks in which we end up with no witnesses, say, on Wednesday. And not to have weeks in which we think of being able of finishing the witnesses we have present here in The Hague and finding us in the impossibility of doing so. So we need to cooperate -- I'm not alleging that you're not cooperating. Don't misunderstand me. But what I'm saying is we need to be more precise. I need more information, if you can give it to us, which would put me in a position to make sure at least on -- with sufficient advance notice of one week to two weeks before where we stand so that if we need to make adjustments, we'll be able to make those adjustments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, you've outlined what is a very difficult problem. And you never know which side of that you should err on, whether you should get too many witnesses here or not enough. And you never know whether it's too many or not enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have been a Defence witness myself, so you're not telling me anything I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This list I gave you today will probably be updated with some frequency, and just rest assured that the time estimates that are on this list are the ones that are currently valid, we think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, whether that remains the case is another question completely. But a lot depends on what goes on between now and a week from now, for instance, as to how long we think some of these witnesses might take. For instance, you mentioned Witness Number 17. It's my recollection that I decided the amount of time that witness would take a long time ago, and then since then we've had discussions with him and we have exhibits that we decided we needed to use with him that tend to expand the amount of time that he'll take and probably the amount of time he will be examined. He was the head of that agency for relocation and exchange, and so I think he's probably likely to be cross-examined at some length also. He may not take that full two or three days, and it may very well be that we'll move Witness Number 29 into that week. It's almost certain we will if we move Witness 5 into the week of 3 November. So my best guess, Your Honour, is that this list is going to be dealt with faster than what it shows, that we'll get through these witnesses faster than this list indicates. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that. I find it difficult to digest, to tell you the truth, Mr. Ackerman. Sorry for interrupting you halfway. But the more I look at your first list, the one with the subject of the testimony listed, if I look at, for example, Witness Number 20 on the fourth page of that document, the very bottom of the page, I mean, you anticipate two days for that gentleman here in the witness box. I personally find it difficult to imagine, even imagine for a moment that we'll finish with that gentleman --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know who that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't have that list here. You can say the name, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Vojo Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's almost certain that he will not come. We can't find him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the same, I mean, I could mention others. My rough guess, having presided over this trial for a year and a half, and having learned a modest -- just a little bit of it, but I can't see, for example, Witness Number 14 testifying for a day and a half only. Same applies to Witness Number 21. You anticipate him to testify for half a day. He was a major in the air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, 14 and 21, neither one are on this current list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. Not this list, I'm worried about the other list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Don't worry about the other list. If you want to worry, worry about this one. If the time comes that you need to worry about the other list, I'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But right now, you don't need to worry about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I take matters one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One by one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, unfortunately I've forgotten what the first matter Your Honour raised was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first matter is there are 43 other witnesses listed here. I do agree and anticipate that we won't see the entire group of 43 witnesses. But if they come, the conservative estimate of hours needed for the testimony according to Mr. Ackerman himself is 40 hours. So that's the first point. MS. KORNER [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what was I going to say? I don't think he will take anything like two to three days if he's just going to deal with what she dealt with. But he deals with other things according to the two-line summary, but until we get a full summary, so it's the problem again of having proper summaries at some stage. So that's the first matter. The second matter in respect of limiting cross-examination, Your Honour, we were limited when Your Honours decided to bring this case to an end on examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have no reason to question the -- or criticise the way you have been conducting the cross-examination so far. We've only had two witnesses, and so I don't think you need to address the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I ever come to the stage, my colleagues and myself, to address you on this or to give you a directive, we'll -- but I don't anticipate that. I don't think for a moment that I can accuse either Mr. Ackerman, Mr. Cunningham in the course of the case of the Prosecution of having abused of the "right" to cross-examine. And I certainly have no reason to criticise you at this early stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, all I was going to say is I would hope that Mr. Ackerman would know all of us well enough to know that we would never deliberately seek to prevent him calling the evidence that he wants to because of time limits. Your Honour, then the Glamoc, Laktas, and Srbac witnesses, Mr. Ackerman explained what he's just said, and I explained it's not as simple as that because you cannot somehow see the interaction without knowing what actually happened in the municipality. The reason I would like to know, and it cannot be that difficult for Mr. Ackerman to let us know whether these witnesses are going to be called or not by the beginning of November, in fact, the week of the 3rd of November, is because we propose to use the adjournment that Your Honour granted Mr. Ackerman to make investigations. It's the best opportunity we have. I do not want, as I said, to waste unnecessary money and resources if in the end, it's one of the witnesses that we're going to drop. Mr. Ackerman's going to drop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I find that to be a reasonable request. We don't need to go further with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honour, I hear what Mr. Ackerman says on, for example, Vojo Kupresanin. For the less-major witnesses, of course, we don't expect an answer, but if there are major witnesses on Mr. Ackerman's list that he knows already he will not be calling, we would be grateful to be informed because otherwise it's a lot of resources being poured into something that's unnecessary. Your Honour, were there any other matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you've covered them all. That's what I think anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to say it's a 100 per cent certainty with regard to Kupresanin. We can't find him. He may -- believe he has been indicted and went into hiding. The Prosecution found him at one point, and we thought he would be easy to find, but he's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we found him by sending a letter to the Republika Srpska authorities together with a summons, but this was back in 2001 so I don't know what's happened since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Veljko Kondic, do you expect to bring him over?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's about a 50/50 possibility, Your Honour. We haven't decided on him yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have one last request. Does Mr. Ackerman know yet who his experts will be for the military and police? I don't think we were provided with those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're still waiting for those. We are still waiting for those, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We had a military expert all lined up. He had agreed. We had gotten his resume. We were getting ready to notify everyone. Then he sent an email saying that he had changed his mind and wouldn't and has recommended a couple of other people who might be willing to take his place. We're in the process of contacting them. That's about as far as I can go. I don't know what the status is of the police expert. I think we're still trying to find a particular person that we wanted to use. Let me just check. No, we have no news about that yet, Your Honour. I'll expedite that and let everybody know by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. There is, for example, Witness Number 50, I cannot mention the name because you yourself asked not to publicly disclose his name, and the following witness, Number 51.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 50, Your Honour, is to be called the 1st of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I want to make sure that he is still coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, he's still coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And 51 may also be one witness that will take longer than you indicate one day. And 55?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he will take longer than a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure. It's almost common sense that he will. 55 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again, you're worrying about the list that I told you not to worry about. If you'll tell me who those people are, I may be able to give you some information. Can we go into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we can go into private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My instinct tells me to -- I'm taking your word not to worry for the time being on the additional list. What I am asking of you, Mr. Ackerman, is to continue this exchange of information on the situation as it pertains particularly in the next couple of weeks, which would enable not only the Prosecution to know exactly how to prepare, but also us to know -- to be in a better position to plan for the after-January period in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you can I think very safely plan that the case will end when you decreed it will end, if not before, and it will probably be before. So I know you worry about things like that. I'd like to relieve you as much as I can because worry is not good for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will understand it's not a question -- I'm not the kind of person who is going to die because of worrying. I can assure you. But on the other hand, you will understand that in my position as Presiding Judge, and the two Judges who sit with me in this trial, we are also ourselves accountable. And if I have two documents which, taken together, in no way can convince anyone that the case for the Defence could be finished by the end of January, I am duty-bound to ask for explanations, which I did this morning. And I am glad that you have given me the explanations that I needed, so that neither of us, or none of us can be exposed to any criticism later on. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a suggestion. If Mr. Ackerman has problems in finding witnesses, it may be we're able to assist through our offices in Banja Luka. And certainly if he wants, we can make inquiries ourselves as to where Mr. Kupresanin is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that is the end. So next week, this coming week, we start with the cross-examination of the military expert. We'll be sitting, I think, in the morning. Can you check for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Any chance for another Court? I think -- doesn't Milosevic get three days off next week or something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, let's see -- no, because -- Monday, 27th, when are we sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In the morning in Courtroom II, all week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then do I have the sentencing hearing in Nikolic in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. And that goes for the entire week. Next week I will be sitting with you in the morning, and then an entire sitting in the afternoon in another case. So it will be a tiring week. But that needs to be done. So I would appreciate your full cooperation because it will be a very tiring week for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in terms of some of these issues that keep rising with regard to the Defence case, I do need to -- for you to really understand as clearly as I can make it that we do not have the personnel necessary to do everything that needs to be done. We have to prioritise. And right now, our priority is the exhibit list. And that's what we're doing. And because of that, the witness summaries aren't getting done. We have to drop something when we have to do one thing. We just don't have the people to do all of this. Our interns are even working more hours than they're supposed to be working for us to try to help us get all these tasks done. I assure you we're doing the best we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate you have difficulties, Mr. Ackerman. I'm not saying that you don't. The moment I convince myself and Judge Janu and Judge Taya decide to agree with me that you are taking advantage, then I will step down on you. But I have no reason to believe that you are taking advantage or that not making available the entire list of documents at the present moment is abusive or -- anyway, I'm not happy with it because I still believe that you have had a year and a half in which to decide at least on a good number of documents that you had in mind or that you intended to make use of. But as I said before, I have been Defence counsel myself for a few years, and I do realise that in any trial, the situation changes from sometimes one hour to -- one moment to the next and that some documents that you had in mind of using, you don't need any further. And others that you would like to use, you know where they are, but are not readily available. So I do know that, and I appreciate that. But on the other hand, the situation is -- I look at it also from another point of view. You keep stressing the point that there is no equality of arms, no parity of arms between the Prosecution and the Defence. And possibly to an extent, in some areas, definitely the Prosecution is much better equipped than any Defence team can be. But that's not the beginning or the end of the story. There is the question of disclosure of documents. And until and unless the Defence opens its archives also to the Prosecutor, which can be done only in certain limited cases, there's no reciprocity, and definitely the Defence is in a better position than the Prosecution is from that point of view. So I don't fancy at all the idea of depriving the Prosecution from something that they are entitled to according to the rules. In order to accept that, there must be special circumstances. And my first duty would be, if there are special circumstances, to ask you to make a greater effort to try and bring everything in line with the requirements of the rules. It's not my style to impose anything until I really feel that the moment has come when I do have to. And I don't think the moment has come as yet. But I ask for your cooperation, Mr. Ackerman, because this is something that I share the concerns of the Prosecution about. I mean, I don't want anyone to accuse me later on of having deliberately closed a blind eye on this matter, especially if the Prosecution at any particular stage in time, now or later, stand up and suggests that they are being prejudiced by the nondisclosure of the list. So I would honestly like you to address and give this matter your earlier attention. And I am glad I heard you say you are giving it priority. Having said that, is there anything else we need to address, Ms. Korner? Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we spoke to Mr. Ackerman, and I understand he's going to email his list to us, provisional list for documents for Mr. Brown, and then maybe about -- some more added for the weekend. But that's the one thing we asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: According to you, you are put in the position where you can do your work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this hasn't arisen, and I'm not pre-empting. I raised the matters Tuesday or Wednesday because I was concerned that we'd only had a sudden list. But I understand Mr. Ackerman's -- we've spoken together, and he is working on it. Certainly I'm not taking any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you keep discussing these as we go along, these matters as we go along. Yes, thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was working on the list since early this morning. I think I'm up to Exhibit Number 255 or something like that. I can send that list to the Prosecutor at any time but I don't think it's of much value without also having the documents, and that's where the bottleneck is right now. We have to make ten copies of each one, and that's an enormous task, but that's what we're doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's all for the day and for the week. Tomorrow we are not sitting as you know. We will reconvene Monday with the cross-examination of the military expert. I don't know which courtroom we are sitting in in the morning on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This one again. And in the afternoon, we are sitting in the sentencing hearing in which Court? Courtroom I, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If Milosevic is only two days next week, can we take that courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it is at all possible, yes. Kelly, is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'll have to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it is possible, we'll take Courtroom I. It's much better than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Especially with the expert witness because it's going to be a very paper-heavy case and there are going to be binders all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, there will be somebody present for the military expert's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have already decreed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Your Honour, we will need more space if at all possible on Monday and Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So we stand adjourned until Monday, 9.00 in the morning. Thank you.
